New research using computer analysis suggests that William Shakespeare wrote "Double Falsehood" around 1613 with help from John Fletcher, debunking the long-held belief that it was a forgery by Lewis Theobald. The study, published in Psychological Science, found a "landslide" match between the play and Shakespeare's linguistic patterns, though the second half appears to be a collaboration. While the findings may settle the authorship debate, they do not negate Theobald's editorial contributions to the work.

Kenya has frozen 86 bank accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters following the Garissa university attack that killed 147 people. The government is tracking the finances of those tied to the militant group, with the number of frozen accounts expected to rise. This action is part of a broader crackdown that includes airstrikes in Somalia and a $215,000 reward for information on the attack's alleged organizer.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for the 2008 murder of Travis Alexander, after two juries failed to reach a unanimous decision on the death penalty. Judge Sherry Stephens overrode the option of early release, citing the brutality of the crime and Arias's lack of remorse until her sentencing. The case will now move to the Arizona State Prison Complex-Perryville, where Arias will serve her life sentence.

Chinese authorities have detained five women's rights activists, including Wu Rongrong, for planning to protest on International Women's Day against sexual harassment. The women face formal arrest by April 13, a move that coincides with China's push to adopt its first anti-domestic violence law and the 20th anniversary of a major women's rights conference. The crackdown highlights the activists' dual fight against government repression and entrenched gender inequality.

Astrophysicist Amy Mainzer named asteroid 316201 Malala after the education activist, honoring her recovery from a Taliban attack and her advocacy for girls' education. The asteroid, located between Mars and Jupiter, is about 4 kilometers in diameter and circles the sun every five and a half years. Mainzer chose the name to recognize Malala's contributions, noting that very few asteroids honor women, particularly women of color.

Emy Afalava, born in American Samoa, is suing the federal government to be recognized as a U.S. citizen despite being born on U.S. soil. His case highlights a longstanding contradiction where the 14th Amendment grants citizenship to those born in the U.S., yet territorial residents like Afalava are routinely denied these rights. The article draws a parallel to historical injustices like the Dred Scott and Gonzalez cases, where the Supreme Court previously excluded Black Americans and Puerto Ricans from full citizenship based on race.

Over the past year, more than 25,000 people have been infected with Ebola, with over 10,000 fatalities, leaving survivors with lasting health and social challenges. Although the epidemic's intensity has decreased and new cases have dropped to their lowest level since 2014, the virus persists in West Africa, where new infections and unsafe burials continue to pose risks of resurgence.

Attorney General Eric Holder issued a memo prohibiting all Justice Department employees, including FBI and DEA agents, from soliciting prostitution regardless of its legality, citing its link to human trafficking. The directive follows a report revealing DEA agents abroad attended sex parties with cartel-paid prostitutes, and applies to all times during employment, including off-duty periods. Violators face suspension or termination.

Nashville prosecutors have been offering female sterilization as part of plea deals, sparking public outrage and comparisons to eugenics history. While the practice is voluntary and differs from past forced sterilizations, it raises constitutional questions regarding the Eighth Amendment and whether such punishments can be constitutionally waived.

The Boston Marathon bomber was found guilty on all counts, but the article argues that preventing future violence requires understanding the complex factors of radicalization rather than attributing it to religion. It highlights that young Muslims like Tsarnaev are often driven to extremism by a sense of grievance stemming from ongoing geopolitical conflicts and perceived attacks on their community. Ultimately, the piece suggests that addressing the root causes of radicalization—rather than viewing Islam as inherently violent—is key to making America safer.

The article highlights the Walter Scott shooting as a rare case where a bystander's video provided clear evidence of police misconduct, contrasting it with the broader lack of data on police killings. It argues that the 1994 Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act, which mandates the Justice Department to track police use of force, has been largely ignored, leaving the U.S. without comprehensive data on racial bias or training practices. Without this data, the nation cannot determine if excessive force is linked to specific policies or systemic bias.

Apple released a new mobile operating system update featuring a diverse array of emojis with varying skin tones, hair colors, and same-sex couple options, sparking both celebration and controversy. The update has already ignited debate, particularly regarding the inclusion of Santa Claus and the absence of redhead emojis, while highlighting the broader cultural significance of representation in digital communication.

Hillary Clinton's 2016 presidential run is framed as a pivotal moment for gender equality, where a victory would mark a historic step forward but risk complacency, while a defeat would reinforce the notion that women cannot win national elections. The article argues that Clinton's unique profile makes her an imperfect standard for judging women's electability, as her name recognition and baggage differ from other female candidates. Ultimately, her candidacy serves as a "barometer" for the state of women's political inclusion in the U.S., regardless of the outcome.

NBC's "A.D. The Bible Continues" premieres Sunday at 9 p.m. ET, serving as a 12-week sequel to the History Channel's "The Bible" that picks up after Jesus' resurrection. Meanwhile, AMC's "Mad Men" begins its final episodes this Sunday, concluding the story of Don Draper and the series' ensemble cast.

The Pentagon released a map showing coalition forces have retaken 25-30% of Iraqi territory from ISIS, primarily in central and northern regions. However, a counterinsurgency expert notes that these territorial gains are largely conventional pushes against ISIS's front lines, rather than the disruptive "maneuver warfare" needed to dismantle the group's command and supply chains.

Arsenal kept their title hopes alive with a 1-0 win over Burnley, moving to within four points of leaders Chelsea ahead of a crucial clash next week. Meanwhile, Aston Villa secured vital points in the relegation battle with a win over Tottenham, while Crystal Palace moved clear of the drop zone with a victory over Sunderland.

It contends that body cameras serve as an effective tool to de-escalate tensions, reduce use-of-force incidents, and restore public confidence in law enforcement, despite the costs of implementation. Ultimately, the author posits that while body cameras are a necessary interim measure, they cannot solve the deeper issue of systemic bias against Black men within the justice system.

Recent statistics show that 8 out of 10 American taxpayers receive a refund averaging around $3,000, making tax season a "happy spending spree" despite the system's inherent complexities and biases. While the process has been simplified by free filing software, the article notes that the tax code remains biased against two-worker marriages and the wealthy, who benefit from untaxed capital gains.

Yarmouk camp, once home to over 100,000 people, has become a hellscape of siege and bombardment where only about 18,000 remain. Residents face extreme deprivation, with ISIS fighters recently storming the area and unleashing violence before withdrawing, leaving the district under the control of al-Qaeda-linked groups. International aid is severely restricted, leaving trapped civilians with no food or water as the conflict grinds down the neighborhood's buildings and population.

The 2015 MTV Movie Awards were defined by Amy Schumer's sharp opening monologue and Channing Tatum's surprise twerk for Jennifer Lopez, though the night was marred by an awkward archery mishap and a controversial "Gone Girl" joke that fell flat with the audience. While Rebel Wilson's "Pitch Perfect 2" gag and the "Centuries" vs. "Trap Queen" medley provided highlights, technical gaffes like the kiss cam and Kevin Hart's award presentation left some moments feeling forced. Marvel Studios unveiled the official look of Paul Bettany's Vision ahead of "Avengers: Age of Ultron," while Bryan Singer confirmed Ben Hardy as the new Angel for "X-Men: Apocalypse." Additionally, the "Fantastic Four" reboot revealed The Thing's CGI design, and a photoshopped "Daredevil" suit was officially debunked by Marvel.

Ursula Ward delivered an emotional statement in court following the conviction of Aaron Hernandez, describing her son Odin Lloyd as the "backbone of the family" and the man who kept his sisters together. Lloyd, a 27-year-old landscaping worker and former semi-pro football player, was killed in 2013, and his mother expressed that while she misses him deeply, she finds strength in the belief she will see him again. The sentencing brings closure to a case that has deeply affected Lloyd's family, who remember him as a hard worker and devoted relative.

Former New England Patriots star Aaron Hernandez will need to keep his lawyers after being convicted of murder, as he faces three additional trials: a criminal case for the 2012 double homicide of Daniel de Abreu and Safiro Furtado, and two civil lawsuits. Prosecutors allege Hernandez fatally shot the two men during a dispute near a Boston nightclub, while a separate civil case involves a man who claims Hernandez wounded him in a Miami limousine in 2013. The new season of "Orphan Black" premieres Saturday, introducing male clones and promising more complex clone scenes, while Tatiana Maslany teases further boundary-pushing performances. Meanwhile, "Turn: Washington's Spies" returns with new historical figures like Benedict Arnold, and "Game of Thrones" kicks off its fifth season as one of the year's biggest premieres.

Alyssa Milano was furious after Heathrow Airport workers allegedly confiscated her pumped breast milk and its cooler while she was traveling with her husband. She criticized the airport's policy, noting that while the UK Department of Transport allows breast milk quantities larger than 100ml through security, the staff ignored these rules. This incident follows a similar 2011 case where a blogger mom had her milk seized under comparable circumstances.

Ten years after Centre County District Attorney Ray Gricar vanished, his case remains unsolved despite extensive searches, digital forensics, and numerous leads. Investigators have considered suicide, foul play, or a voluntary disappearance, but the lack of hard evidence leaves the mystery largely theoretical. While his laptop and car were recovered from the Susquehanna River, they yielded little conclusive information, and his fate continues to baffle those close to the case.

As Americans mark the 150th anniversary of Abraham Lincoln's death, the article highlights how his Midwestern roots shaped his belief that the Union was indivisible and older than the states themselves. Lincoln viewed the Mississippi River as a critical geostrategic chokepoint, arguing that no state could secede without threatening the nation's economic and political integrity. He insisted the Union created the states, a claim that contradicted the views of those, like Robert E. Lee, who believed states like Virginia predated the United States.

Marvel's "Daredevil" has arrived on Netflix to largely positive reception, with critics praising Charlie Cox's performance and the show's faithful adaptation of the character's origins. The series distinguishes itself by launching directly into action without a lengthy origin story, earning a 94% positive rating on Rotten Tomatoes for its well-scripted narrative and strong choreography.

Located in rural Florida, the Ringling Bros. Center for Elephant Conservation houses 29 elephants and plans to expand to 42 by 2018. The facility was established to provide a permanent home for elephants as the circus phased out their use due to legal challenges and inconsistent regulations across cities. The center also serves as a research hub focused on breeding and preserving the Asian elephant species.

Two years after the Boston Marathon bombings, Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was convicted on 30 charges related to the attack, with the jury now deliberating his punishment, including the possibility of the death penalty. While the city held somber ceremonies to honor the victims and observe "One Boston Day," the focus remained on the resilience of the community rather than the convicted bomber's fate.

University of Nairobi students panicked and injured themselves after mistaking a faulty electrical cable explosion for a terror attack, occurring less than two weeks after the Garissa university massacre. At least one person died and dozens were hospitalized, with the university confirming the incident was an accident and power supply will be restored after repairs.

Reserve Deputy Robert Bates turned himself in to face second-degree manslaughter charges after fatally shooting Eric Harris, whom he mistakenly shot with a handgun instead of his Taser during an undercover sting. Bates surrendered Tuesday morning and posted $25,000 bail, maintaining that the shooting was unintentional as his attorneys argue it was an "excusable homicide." Harris' family, while acknowledging other good officers, demand an independent investigation, questioning why a 73-year-old volunteer reserve with limited recent training was involved in a high-risk arrest.

Iman and Siham Hashi, former refugees from Mogadishu, are now a pop duo signed to Warner Brothers, blending Afro-pop with hip-hop and African percussion. Their music reflects their journey from a war-torn homeland to a successful career, and they actively advocate for refugees through their work with the UNHCR.

Hundreds of Iraqi troops have been deployed to reinforce defenses at the Baiji oil refinery, which ISIS has been attacking since Saturday. The reinforcements, including federal police and Shiite militia fighters, are attempting to push ISIS out of the facility to prevent damage to a key domestic fuel source. Iraqi officials currently deny that ISIS has taken control of the refinery, insisting their forces remain in full command.

Tokyo Electric Power Company abandoned a robotic probe inside the Fukushima Daiichi reactor after it was blocked by debris, having only covered two-thirds of its planned route. The mission was intended to assess radiation levels and debris spread, but a fallen object left the device stranded. TEPCO decided to cut the robot's cable, noting it had successfully collected data from 14 of the 18 targeted locations before the operation was halted.

More than 500 Houthi rebels have been killed in Saudi-led airstrikes, which have also resulted in the deaths of three Saudi soldiers and over 380 civilians. The nine-nation coalition has conducted over 1,200 airstrikes since March 26 to prevent the rebels from advancing south, while the UN reports that 25 million Yemenis require urgent humanitarian aid.

A Hong Kong bakery is struggling to keep up with demand for its "Jenny's cookies," which have sparked a black market where people pay premiums to skip long lines. The original shop has even posted warnings against buying counterfeit versions, as resellers mark up the treats by 70%. This frenzy reflects a global trend where food crazes, like cronuts and ramen burgers, captivate the public before quickly fading.

An explosion outside a bus station in Gombe, Nigeria, killed at least five people and injured over a dozen others. The blast was caused by a woman who left an explosives-laden handbag near a bus before fleeing the scene, and while no group has claimed responsibility, Boko Haram is the main suspect.

Brett McGurk, the Obama administration's point man against ISIS, described the group's threat as "off the charts historically," noting that over 20,000 foreign fighters have joined the conflict in Syria—double the number that fought in Afghanistan in the 1980s. The first trailer for "Amy: The Girl Behind the Name" was released Thursday, offering a glimpse into the late singer's early career and her ambivalence toward fame. Set for a UK release on July 3, the documentary seeks to "truly capture not just the great artist that she was, but also the funny and loving person that most people didn't get a chance to know," featuring previously unseen footage and tracks. Endorsed by Winehouse's family, the film aims to honor her musical legacy without sensationalizing her struggles.

Federal Judge George A. O'Toole instructed jurors in the Boston Marathon bombing trial to avoid attending the race or related events during the sentencing phase, which begins April 21, to prevent any prejudicial influence on the death penalty decision. The judge's warning comes as the jury, which already convicted Dzhokhar Tsarnaev on all 30 counts, will now determine his sentence, with the maximum penalty being death. A former U.S. Army enlistee was arrested for attempting to detonate a car bomb at Fort Riley, believing he was acting on ISIS orders. The "bomb" was actually an inert device assembled by undercover agents, and the suspect was charged after making inflammatory comments on Facebook about attacking American soldiers. A second man was also charged for failing to report the plot to authorities.

Gwyneth Paltrow is participating in the #FoodBankNYCChallenge to experience life on a food stamp budget, spending just under $30 on groceries for one week. The challenge, which limits participants to $1.38 per meal, aims to raise awareness of the struggles families face following recent cuts to food assistance programs.

A rowing team's practice was interrupted when a swarm of Asian carp leaped from Creve Coeur Lake and attacked their boat, causing panic among the athletes. Though no one was physically injured, the incident left the rowers startled and the boat smelling strongly of fish.

Muhammadu Buhari has won Nigeria's presidency, defeating incumbent Goodluck Jonathan in a historic democratic transition of power. The former military ruler, who previously governed in the 1980s, campaigned on an anti-corruption platform and pledged to address Boko Haram violence and economic challenges. Buhari is set to be sworn in on May 29, marking the first time Nigeria's opposition has defeated the ruling party in elections.

As ISIS fighters advanced into Ramadi, thousands of civilians fled on foot across the only bridge into Baghdad, leaving behind homes and loved ones. With security forces collapsing and the government restricting vehicle access to prevent bombs, many exhausted refugees piled into carts or walked for miles to escape the violence.

Amina Ali Qassim and her family fled their Yemeni island home as Saudi airstrikes began, escaping just before their house was destroyed. They endured a harrowing five-hour crossing of the Bab al-Mandab Strait in a crowded boat to reach temporary shelter in Djibouti, where they now face an uncertain future with two daughters still trapped in Taiz.

Georgia Governor Nathan Deal signed "Haleigh's Hope Act," legalizing low-THC cannabis oil to treat medication-resistant epilepsy. The law allows families like the Coxes, who previously had to relocate to Colorado, to receive treatment in-state, significantly improving the quality of life for children like Haleigh. The bill marks a major shift for the state, enabling patients to stay home while accessing much-needed medical care.

Photographer Carolina Sandretto documents the "solares," crumbling Cuban apartment buildings where multiple generations and families cohabitate due to housing shortages following the 1959 revolution. Using a vintage Hasselblad camera, Sandretto captures intimate, timeless moments of daily life amid disintegrating surroundings, aiming to preserve a way of life she fears will change as U.S.-Cuba relations normalize.

The White House argues it can bypass congressional approval for the Iran nuclear deal, but historical precedent suggests securing legislative consent would make the agreement far more durable. While the administration frames the deal as a nonbinding executive agreement to avoid political gridlock, the push for congressional review—exemplified by the Corker bill—highlights the significant political risks of sidestepping the legislative branch. Ultimately, moving forward without Congress risks creating a less stable diplomatic breakthrough that could face legal challenges and lack the enduring legitimacy of a treaty ratified by the Senate.

Lady Antebellum singer Hillary Scott's tour bus caught fire on a Texas freeway Thursday morning, but all passengers were safely evacuated. The driver stopped the vehicle after a rear tire blew out, and the fire erupted shortly after everyone had exited the bus. The band is set to perform at the Academy of Country Music Awards on Sunday despite the incident.

The Senate passed a bipartisan Medicare reform bill with a 92-8 vote, permanently fixing the "doc fix" payment system and extending the Children's Health Insurance Program for two years. The legislation, which now heads to President Obama for signature, faced opposition from some conservatives who argued it added too much to the national debt without sufficient reforms. The bill's passage prevents immediate payment cuts to physicians that would have occurred had the temporary fix expired.

A woman snorkeling in Bali found a gold ring engraved with "Happy 70th Birthday 2009" and, using Facebook, tracked down the Australian owner, Joe Langley, who had lost it nine months prior while snorkeling in the same spot. After the ring was professionally cleaned, Roxy Walsh met Joe and his wife Jenny in Noosa to return the sentimental heirloom.

At least 12 people were killed in separate attacks on a police station, a checkpoint, and a highway in Egypt's northern Sinai, claimed by ISIS affiliate Ansar Beit Al-Maqdis. The violence included a car bomb at a police station in Al-Arish that killed six and injured 40, and an attack on a military convoy that killed a first lieutenant, a sergeant, and four conscripts. The attacks occurred as the military announced a reshuffle of senior positions amid an ongoing decade-long Islamist insurgency.

HLN's #MeForReal campaign encourages people to share unfiltered, real-life moments to combat online judgment, sparked by singer P!nk's positive response to body-shaming comments about her post-cancer benefit photo. The article highlights how P!nk's confident rebuttal inspired fans to embrace their own "squishiness" and imperfections, ultimately turning the haters' negativity into more support for the artist.

Cynthia Lennon, who married John Lennon in 1962 and stood by him as he rose to fame with the Beatles, died Wednesday at age 75 following a battle with cancer. Her son Julian was at her bedside, and the family asked for privacy during this difficult time.

The article highlights the significance of the first handshake between President Obama and Cuban President Raul Castro at the Summit of the Americas in Panama, viewing it as a potential turning point for U.S.-Cuba relations. However, it warns that the U.S. must actively work to reverse its declining influence in Latin America, which has been ceded to rivals like China, Russia, and Iran. Obama faces the challenge of leveraging the summit to strengthen regional ties while avoiding the diplomatic blunders that have plagued previous summits, such as the controversy in Cartagena.

Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott announced a "no jab, no pay" policy that removes the conscientious objector exemption from welfare benefits, threatening up to $11,000 in annual child care payments for parents who refuse to vaccinate their children. The policy, effective January 2016, aims to increase immunization rates after a decade-long rise in unvaccinated children, though it has sparked opposition from over 7,000 petitioners. A New Jersey auction house removed 24 lots of Japanese-American internment camp artifacts from its April 17 sale following a public outcry led by a Change.org petition and actor George Takei. The items, inherited from historian Allen Eaton's estate, were intended to be sold but were pulled after community members argued they should be returned or displayed in a museum rather than auctioned. The auction house stated they hope the controversy sparks a broader discussion on the ethics of selling items born from "man's inhumanity to man."

In the Shariya refugee camp, Yazidi women like Hanan recount their enslavement by ISIS following the Sinjar assault. After being separated from their families, Hanan and other girls were subjected to beatings, threats, and sexual slavery in Mosul, eventually escaping by crawling out a window into ISIS territory. Though physically free, Hanan remains mentally tormented, living in fear of ISIS fighters and carrying the trauma of her captivity.

A Los Angeles judge ordered V. Stiviano to repay over $2.6 million in gifts given to her by Donald Sterling, following a lawsuit by his wife, Rochelle "Shelly" Sterling, who accused Stiviano of targeting wealthy older men. Stiviano had received luxury items including two Bentleys, a Range Rover, and a Ferrari, but the court ruled she must return the funds, which Shelly Sterling called a "victory" for the family. Washington Post bureau chief Jason Rezaian has been detained in Iran for nearly nine months on unspecified espionage charges, which his family and the U.S. State Department have called "absurd." Despite appeals from figures like Muhammad Ali and repeated requests for bail and legal access, Rezaian remains imprisoned while his wife was released on bail last October.

NBA player Thabo Sefolosha suffered a season-ending fractured fibula and ligament damage during his arrest in New York, which he claims was caused by police. The Atlanta Hawks guard stated the injury "was caused by the police," and will miss the playoffs as he undergoes surgery. Sefolosha and his teammate Pero Antic were charged with misdemeanors after the incident, but maintain their innocence and will contest the charges in court.

Georgian chess grandmaster Gaioz Nigalidze was banned from the Dubai Open after he was caught using a smartphone hidden in a bathroom stall to consult a chess analysis app during his game. Officials discovered the device after Tigran Petrosian of Armenia grew suspicious of Nigalidze's frequent trips to the restroom. The infraction has been reported to the International Chess Federation, which could lead to a three-year suspension for the player.

Al Qaeda has suffered a significant decapitation, with the confirmed deaths of two senior leaders in CIA drone strikes and a Pakistani military raid. The losses, including the group's South Asia deputy and a key operative, underscore al Qaeda's decline from a global threat to a Pakistan-focused organization with virtually no capacity to attack the West. This decline leaves Ayman al-Zawahiri as the group's primary remaining leader, as al Qaeda's focus has shifted toward holding hostages rather than conducting external operations.

A new report claims Tulsa County Sheriff's Office supervisors were ordered to falsify training records for volunteer deputy Robert Bates, who is accused of killing Eric Harris; three supervisors who refused were reassigned. The Sheriff's Office denied the allegations, calling them unsubstantiated, while Bates' attorney cited a former employee's affidavit as the source. The investigation into the shooting continues to highlight concerns over Bates' qualifications and missing training documentation.

Eleven TV5Monde channels went dark due to a "powerful cyberattack," with the network attributing the hack to an Islamist group. While no group has claimed responsibility, ISIS imagery appeared on social media as teams worked to restore service. The outage affected the network's websites and social media, impacting its global reach of 260 million homes.

Hillary Clinton's campaign team met in Brooklyn to finalize strategy ahead of her official announcement, distributing a "values statement" to avoid past mistakes. The campaign, branded "Hillary for America," aims to unite around a message of prosperity while emphasizing humility and discipline to win over voters in early primary states.

John Helinski, a homeless man who had been without identification for three years, was recently able to secure housing and Social Security benefits after a police officer and case worker helped him navigate bureaucratic hurdles. With his identification and records finally sorted out, the Social Security Administration began paying him the back benefits he was owed, allowing him to look forward to purchasing his own home.

A natural gas line explosion at a Fresno County law enforcement shooting range injured 11 people, including inmates on a work detail and a county road worker. The blast, which occurred near a front loader, sparked a fire that required emergency surgery for two critically injured individuals, while others suffered burns and hearing issues.

U.S. military personnel and foreign volunteers are training Iraqi and Kurdish forces to combat ISIS, with some former soldiers like Jordan Matson joining groups like the YPG despite legal restrictions. While the Kurdish Peshmerga generally reject foreign fighters, preferring to rely on their own ranks, trainers like Ian Bradbury are supplementing U.S. efforts to develop local capabilities. The article highlights a complex landscape where individual motivation clashes with official policies and regional pride.

Vin Diesel's claim that "Furious 7" will win Best Picture is notable not just for its audacity, but because the film stands in stark contrast to the Academy's recent history of homogeneity. While the Oscars faced backlash for "#OscarsSoWhite," "Furious 7" distinguishes itself with a racially and ethnically diverse cast that reflects the international makeup of its filming locations. The film's success and inclusive casting serve as a pointed rebuttal to the notion that blockbuster action movies cannot be progressive or award-worthy.

The California Department of Public Health declared the measles outbreak over on Friday, 42 days after the last known case of the B3 strain. The outbreak, which began at Disney theme parks in December, resulted in 131 cases, with 70% of the 81 patients with known vaccination status being unvaccinated.

Thousands of South Africans marched in Durban to protest xenophobic violence that has killed five people, joining an online campaign using hashtags like #PeaceMarch. Activist Tim Flack has filed a complaint against Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini for allegedly fueling hate by calling foreigners "lice," arguing that social media posts alone are insufficient to combat deep-seated resentment. While organizations like the Gift of Givers Foundation provide aid to refugees, many question whether current efforts are enough to address the underlying tensions between nationals and immigrants.

A Long Island cardiologist, Dr. Anthony Moschetto, was charged with plotting to have a rival doctor hurt or killed. Prosecutors allege Moschetto solicited two men to commit arson and assault, offering cash and blank prescriptions in exchange. He was released on $2 million bond while facing multiple charges including conspiracy and weapons offenses.

The U.N. Security Council voted to impose an arms embargo on Houthi rebels and their allies, including former President Ali Abdullah Saleh, in an effort to raise the cost of their advance on Yemen. The resolution also demands the Houthis pull back from violence and includes sanctions to control terrorism, though Russia abstained over concerns about the sanctions. Additionally, Egypt agreed to form a joint military commission with Saudi Arabia and announced it would dispatch naval ships to help halt the rebel advance.

A trailer for Zack Snyder's "Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice" leaked online before being removed, featuring Ben Affleck and Henry Cavill. The footage, which was set to debut in Imax theaters on Monday, shows the two superheroes clashing amid public debate over their roles as saviors.

The jury in the Aaron Hernandez trial deliberated for over 35 hours across seven days before convicting the former NFL star of first-degree murder in the death of Odin Lloyd. Jurors described the process as grueling, noting they filled multiple notebooks with evidence and struggled to reach a unanimous decision. Despite the emotional weight, they expressed satisfaction with their verdict and maintained they approached the case with open minds throughout the months-long trial.

A third suspect, George Davon Kennedy, was arrested in connection with an alleged spring break gang rape on Panama City Beach, bringing the total number of arrests to three. Authorities are pressing charges against the men, who are students at various universities, while the victim, who was allegedly drugged and assaulted in broad daylight, is cooperating with the investigation.

The Defense Department announced the exhumation of remains from nearly 400 unaccounted-for service members of the USS Oklahoma, which sank during the Pearl Harbor attack. The goal is to identify most of the sailors and Marines using modern forensic technology, with next of kin being notified starting Tuesday. While not all will be individually identified, the department aims to provide resolution to as many families as possible.

Thousands of Syrian and Palestinian refugees trapped in Yarmouk camp have suffered "untold indignities," with U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon describing it as "the deepest circle of hell." The article highlights two infants, Jihad and Mohammad, as "miracle children" whose survival underscores the urgent need for humanitarian access and political will to protect civilians trapped in the conflict.

South African authorities detained a 15-year-old girl at Cape Town International Airport after she was found attempting to travel to join ISIS. The minister stated she had been radicalized online through social media interactions and extremist material, and she has since been released into her family's care while investigations continue.

A 20-year-old murder suspect, Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, was removed from a courtroom after he swore at a judge and attempted to flip a table during a first-degree murder hearing. Stancil is accused of killing Ron Lane, a college employee, and investigators are probing the incident as a possible hate crime, as Stancil has previously expressed hatred toward gay people. He was arrested in Florida and, after initially refusing a court-appointed lawyer, later agreed to representation.

Robert Bates, a reserve deputy charged in the death of Eric Harris, claims he accidentally shot Harris while reaching for his Taser, stating "it can happen to anyone." Despite Bates asserting he completed required training, the sheriff's office cannot locate his firearms certification records, and officials are investigating allegations that his training records were forged.

Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta declared three days of national mourning after an Al-Shabaab attack on a university in Garissa killed 147 people, many of whom were students. The suspected mastermind, Mohamed Mohamud, is a former teacher at a local Islamic school who is believed to have joined the militant group and is now based near the Kenya-Somalia border. Authorities are increasingly concerned about homegrown radicalization, noting that at least one of the gunmen was also Kenyan, highlighting the difficulty of countering terrorism from within communities.

Pope Francis commemorated the 100th anniversary of the Armenian genocide by using the term "genocide" in his speech, but only by quoting his predecessor, Pope John Paul II, to maintain continuity with past Vatican policy. By referencing John Paul's 2001 document, Francis avoided a direct declaration that might have been seen as a policy shift, while still acknowledging the tragedy as "the first genocide of the 20th century." This approach allowed the Pope to honor the Armenian people without provoking the Turkish government, which rejects the genocide label.

The NFL will reinstate Adrian Peterson as an active player on Friday, contingent upon him maintaining counseling and avoiding further conduct violations. The Minnesota Vikings have expressed their eagerness to have him rejoin the team, though Peterson's future participation in offseason workouts remains uncertain.

A Tulsa County reserve deputy, Robert (Bob) Bates, mistakenly shot and killed Eric Courtney Harris during an arrest at a Dollar General store, believing he was deploying his Taser instead of his service weapon. Police reported that Harris, a convicted felon, had fled and resisted arrest, reaching toward his waistband, which led to the altercation where the 73-year-old deputy inadvertently fired his gun. The incident is under investigation, with authorities noting the rapidly evolving nature of the situation and Harris's reported possible influence of PCP at the time of his death.

Chinese police arrested over 133,000 people and seized 43.3 tons of narcotics during a six-month anti-drug campaign, a significant increase from the previous year. The operation resulted in the deaths of nine officers and 657 injuries, while authorities also intensified efforts against online drug trafficking and entertainment industry drug use.

Jack White announced a brief, first-ever acoustic tour to promote "Lazeretto," visiting only five U.S. states he has never played before. The shows will be unannounced day-of, with tickets limited to one per person and priced at just $3.

CNN reports that UNICEF was granted rare access to Sanaa Airport to deliver vital aid amid Yemen's brutal conflict, where a brief, negotiated ceasefire allows for the unloading of emergency supplies. The mission is urgent, as over 15.9 million people are in need of assistance and more than 100,000 have fled their homes since fighting began. However, the humanitarian window is fragile, with hostilities likely to resume quickly, making the delivery of food and medical equipment a race against time for those trapped inside the country.

Tomasz Lazar's new photo series captures the haunting faces of Polish survivors who were deported to Siberia as children during World War II, documenting their traumatic experiences before time runs out. Through intimate portraits and interviews, Lazar preserves their stories to ensure future generations understand the consequences of totalitarianism and the resilience of the human spirit. The project serves as a poignant reminder of a stolen generation, highlighting how these survivors finally found the courage to share their pasts now that the Soviet Union has fallen.

Robert Bates' lawyer released training documents to verify the reserve deputy's qualifications in the fatal shooting of Eric Harris. The records show Bates completed minimal Taser and firearms training, though his attorney claims he met all state requirements. The documents have become central to the case, as the victim's family alleges Bates received preferential treatment due to donations and personal connections.

A naturalized U.S. citizen from Columbus was arrested and pleaded not guilty to charges of providing material support to terrorists and lying to the FBI. The 23-year-old allegedly traveled to Syria for training with the intent to return home and kill Americans, particularly U.S. soldiers, execution style.

The article discusses how Andreas Lubitz, the co-pilot of Germanwings Flight 9525, likely suffered from severe psychiatric issues that went unnoticed despite the rigorous selection and training processes required to become a pilot. It highlights that while the FAA now allows certain medications for depression, Lubitz's case illustrates the dangers of undiagnosed mental illness and the failure of those around him, including his girlfriend, to recognize the red flags before the tragedy occurred.

This week's pop culture highlights included the release of a new "Star Wars: The Force Awakens" trailer and the retirement of supermodel Gisele Bundchen. A viral math problem about "Cheryl's birthday" stumped the internet, while ESPN reporter Britt McHenry faced backlash for an on-air rant after her car was towed. Additionally, the first set of female quintuplets since 1969 were born in Texas, and "Late Late Show" host James Corden paid tribute to "Pretty in Pink" with a Duckie dance.

Warner Bros. and director Michelle MacLaren have mutually parted ways over "creative differences" just months before "Wonder Woman" was set to begin filming. Despite the departure, the film remains on track for a June 23, 2017 release, with Gal Gadot still starring as the Amazon princess while the studio searches for a new director.

A New York jury will deliberate over a verdict in the 1979 disappearance of Etan Patz, 35 years after the case captivated the nation. While Pedro Hernandez has confessed to the crime, his lawyer argues he is mentally incompetent and unable to distinguish reality from false memories. The case remains fraught with legal hurdles, including a judge's ruling that Hernandez's confession was admissible despite his schizophrenia diagnosis.

ABC is developing a revival of "The Muppets," with "Big Bang Theory" co-creator Bill Prady co-writing the pilot. The project is set to film next weekend, but its future depends on Miss Piggy's participation, as her strained relationship with Kermit is currently blocking progress. If ordered to series, the show would reunite the classic characters at ABC Studios, marking a return for Prady, who previously worked for Jim Henson in the 1980s.

The article recounts a woman's personal experience of sexual harassment on a Mumbai train at age 13, noting she remained silent for 25 years. It highlights that 80% of women in Mumbai face street harassment, yet most incidents go unreported due to societal normalization and fear, with many women altering their routines to avoid public spaces. The author argues that confronting this pervasive issue requires women to speak out and recognize their collective power to effect change.

Canadian actor Jonathan Crombie, best known for playing Gilbert Blythe in the "Anne of Green Gables" TV movies, died at age 48 from complications of a brain hemorrhage. His portrayal of the character opposite Megan Follows became iconic, earning him a lasting legacy as a heartthrob and cultural touchstone for fans worldwide.

Al-Shabaab's attack on Garissa University College, which killed 147 people, represents the deadliest assault in Kenya in over a year and a half, surpassing the 2013 Westgate Mall siege. The group, weakened by years of losses in Somalia to African Union forces and U.S. drone strikes, has increasingly targeted "soft" civilian sites rather than military bases, highlighting its diminishing capabilities despite its continued ability to strike at symbolic Kenyan institutions.

Former rap mogul Marion "Suge" Knight was ordered to stand trial for murder and other charges related to a deadly hit-and-run on the "Straight Outta Compton" set, with his bail reduced to $10 million. The judge dismissed one hit-and-run count because California law prohibits multiple charges for the same vehicle, and Knight's fiancée reported his health has improved after he collapsed upon learning of the original bail amount.

National Park Week, running from April 18 to 26, offers free admission to the 128 U.S. national parks that typically charge fees, including popular sites like Yellowstone and Yosemite. The initiative, hosted by the National Park Service and the National Park Foundation, features events like astronomy parties and Junior Ranger activities, with more information available at FindYourPark.com. The campaign encourages visitors to explore and share their experiences using the hashtag #FindYourPark.

The article highlights the severe affordable housing crisis in the U.S., noting that families are spending half their income on rent or living in substandard conditions. It details how the Department of Housing and Urban Development is working to preserve existing affordable housing and public housing stock to prevent further loss of units. The initiative aims to ensure families can invest in their children's future rather than dedicating nearly all their income just to keep a roof over their heads.

An American citizen was shot and wounded in Karachi, Pakistan, while driving from the medical school where she works. Debra Lobo, a 55-year-old vice principal, was targeted by two assailants on a motorcycle who threw pamphlets stating "America should be burnt."

Rolling Stone's "A Rape on Campus" story was found to be journalistic malpractice due to the magazine's failure to verify sources and give the accused a fair chance to respond, leading to its eventual retraction. The Columbia University investigation revealed that reporter Sabrina Rubin Erdely ignored red flags and skipped basic fact-checking, prioritizing the story's publication over accuracy. While the allegations sparked important conversations about campus sexual assault, the magazine's lapses were deemed unacceptable and would be considered failures in any introductory journalism course.

Jon Cryer recreated his iconic "Pretty in Pink" dance with James Corden on "The Late Late Show," fulfilling Corden's childhood dream. The duo performed the famous record-store routine to Otis Redding's "Try a Little Tenderness," delighting fans who grew up with the 1986 film.

The public backlash against "religious freedom" bills in Arkansas and Indiana caught governors off-guard, revealing a growing divide between socially conservative laws and the business community's pushback. Major corporations, from Apple to Marriott, have condemned the legislation, arguing that anti-discrimination policies are essential for attracting younger consumers and the lucrative LGBT travel market. This shift signals that the traditional alliance between the religious right and big business is fracturing as companies prioritize brand loyalty and economic interests over ideological opposition to same-sex marriage.

Ines Dumig's photo series "Apart Together" documents Sahra, a Somali refugee who fled her home at 14, highlighting her resilience and the universal emotions of isolation and the search for identity. The project emerged from Dumig's realization of her own privilege and serves as a broader commentary on the shared human experience of feeling "apart" despite physical distance. Ultimately, the series emphasizes the strength of refugees like Sahra, who, despite bureaucratic dehumanization, strive to build new lives while confronting feelings of "otherness."

Jarret Stoll of the L.A. Kings was arrested in Las Vegas on Friday and charged with possession of controlled substances, including cocaine and ecstasy. He was released on $5,000 bail, and the Kings have launched an internal investigation into the incident.

A man in Arizona fired a stolen rifle into the air at a Walmart before being struck by a police car, an incident that sparked debate over the officer's tactics. The suspect, Mario Valencia, faces multiple charges after police determined the gun's safety lock was loose enough to allow it to fire despite appearing secured. Valencia is currently jailed awaiting further court proceedings.

Two Delaware boys remain comatose and their father is unable to move or speak two weeks after the family fell ill during a trip to the U.S. Virgin Islands, possibly due to pesticide exposure. The family was airlifted to the U.S. after the father was found unconscious and the boys and mother suffered seizures, with the EPA confirming the presence of methyl bromide at their rental villa.

A suicide car bomb attack near the U.S. Consulate in Irbil, Iraq, was claimed by ISIS, resulting in at least four deaths and 18 injuries. While all U.S. Consulate personnel were safe, the blast occurred close to a popular expat area, prompting a joint investigation by the U.S. State Department and Kurdish authorities.

Over 300 suspects have been arrested in South Africa following deadly attacks on foreign nationals that have killed at least five people and forced thousands to flee. The government has condemned the violence, emphasizing that the attacks are unjustifiable and noting that many South Africans have expressed support for the victims. President Jacob Zuma has visited displaced foreigners, and the government has urged citizens to remember the country's history of refuge, as xenophobic sentiment continues to fuel the crisis.

Davion Navar Henry Only, who had spent his entire life in foster care, finally found a permanent family after a viral plea for adoption at a Florida church. With the support of his social worker, Connie Going, and her three children, he was officially adopted on April 22, marking the end of his long journey through the system.

Senator Elizabeth Warren has defiantly vowed to continue challenging Wall Street despite pressure from banks, while Hillary Clinton and other Democratic candidates face a dilemma: addressing economic inequality while relying on Wall Street funding. The article argues that Democratic populism is fundamentally incompatible with the current campaign finance system, which forces candidates to court wealthy donors and corporate interests to win elections, even as they criticize economic disparity.

Saudi Arabia has been conducting airstrikes in Yemen for three weeks to push back Houthi rebels, but the conflict has intensified rather than de-escalated, resulting in a rising death toll and mass displacement. The fighting has raised fears of a broader proxy war between Saudi Arabia and Iran, as the U.N. Security Council recently imposed an arms embargo on the Houthis to curb the violence.

Joy Womack, an American ballerina who left the Bolshoi Ballet Academy in 2013 amid payment disputes, now works as a principal dancer at the Kremlin Ballet Theatre, where she earns roughly $240 a month. She describes her financial situation as difficult due to the weakened Russian ruble, relying on a friend for accommodation and supplementing her income by performing abroad to make ends meet.

Six Minnesota men, ages 19 to 21, were arrested for conspiring to join ISIS, having plotted for 10 months using peer-to-peer recruitment. The group was motivated and persistent, continuing their plans even after co-conspirators were caught, with four appearing in court without bail.

Dr. Sanjay Gupta explores the science behind medical marijuana in his new documentary "Weed 3," addressing its potential to treat conditions like epilepsy, PTSD, and chronic pain while challenging decades of misinformation. He discusses the drug's benefits, risks—particularly regarding brain development—and why it remains a taboo subject in the medical community despite its growing acceptance.

Maggie Doyne, a former New Jersey native, left her comfortable life to establish a children's home and school in Surkhet, Nepal, after witnessing the aftermath of a decade-long civil war. Today, her BlinkNow Foundation supports over 50 children in a communal home and educates more than 350 students at Kopila Valley School, prioritizing family preservation while providing education and care to those in need.

In July 2014, Sierra Sharry and Lane Smith were about to become parents. Sharry was eight months pregnant when Smith fell and hit his head. He was taken to OU Medical Center in Oklahoma City, but he did not survive. Sharry posted on Facebook that July 13th was the worst day of her life because she had lost her best friend and the father of her unborn child. Their son, Taos, was born a few weeks later. When it was time for his six-month pictures, Sharry asked the photographer to make their family complete for just one picture.

By now, you likely have an opinion on Indiana's religious freedom law. Some people support the companies criticizing the law, saying it allows businesses to discriminate against gay and lesbian people. Others, like Indiana Governor Mike Pence, are surprised by the anger and say the law is similar to a federal law and laws in 19 other states. The debate is heated because it involves religious freedom and gay rights, and people argue about what the law really means.

Some fans of Lucille Ball want her statue removed from a park in her hometown. They say the "ugly" likeness does not look like the "I Love Lucy" star. The life-size bronze statue in Celoron, New York, has been compared to Conway Twitty, a snake from "Beetlejuice," and actor Steve Buscemi. Even Mayor Scott Schrecengost says he does not like the statue, which shows Ball holding a bottle of the fictional nutrition elixir Vitameatavegamin. Despite the criticism, the statue has been a tourist attraction in Celoron, the comedian's birthplace, since 2009. People visit to take pictures with it.

For the first time in Nigeria's history, the opposition party defeated the ruling party in an election. Muhammadu Buhari, 72, won the presidency by defeating the current leader, Goodluck Jonathan, by about two million votes.

Nigeria is very important because it has the biggest economy and the most people of any country in Africa. It is also one of Africa's largest oil producers and a major supplier of crude oil to the United States.

CNN reports that Iranians celebrated in the streets after a nuclear deal with world powers. Young people waved flags from their cars and played music. The celebration happened on Vali Asr street in Tehran, where people danced and honked car horns. Some people even waved U.S. dollar bills. The deal is expected to end years of economic sanctions against Iran.

A fourth man has been charged with helping terrorists and trying to join ISIS. Brooklyn Federal Court released the charges on Monday. The new charge was added to a case that already includes three other men. Those three men are Abdurasul Hasanovich Juraboev, Akhror Saidakhmetov, and Abror Habibov. All three have pleaded not guilty. It is not known if the fourth man has been arrested.

A third blood moon appeared in the sky early Saturday. It was the shortest eclipse of a four-part series. The moon fully entered Earth's shadow at 4:58 a.m. Pacific Time (7:58 a.m. ET). This created a total lunar eclipse that lasted nearly five minutes. NASA says this will be the shortest such eclipse of the century. Before, during, and after the total eclipse, the moon turned a burnt-orange color. This is why the event is called a "blood moon." Early risers in North America were able to see it.

Istanbul, Turkey (CNN) Turkish people were very worried on Tuesday. An elderly woman in a headscarf with shopping bags asked, "What is happening? Why can't I get into the subway?" She was one of millions of people confused by the biggest power cut in over ten years. Power was cut off in dozens of cities for hours. Millions of people were affected, including those stuck on trains and subways.

During Holy Week, we are reminded that the Bible asks us to treat workers fairly. Isaiah 58:6 says that true fasting means breaking the chains of injustice, ending workplace exploitation, freeing the oppressed, and canceling debts.

McDonald's recent decision to raise wages for 90,000 employees is a major win for fast-food cooks and cashiers. By standing together, these workers are making it harder for profitable companies to pay wages so low that employees are forced into poverty.

Gov. Jerry Brown of California has ordered mandatory water restrictions because of a drought. This is the first time the state has required residents, businesses, and farms to reduce water use. Brown said the state is in a "new era" where green lawns watered every day are no longer acceptable. The order requires a 25% reduction in water use across the state. This will save about 1.5 million acre-feet of water over the next nine months. (An acre-foot of water is about 325,000 gallons.)

Britons have a short time left to choose who to vote for. Polling stations are getting ready to open across the country. This election could change the political landscape. The campaign has been very short, especially compared to the United States. The vote could give power from David Cameron's Conservative government to the Labour Party, led by Ed Miliband. Or, leaders might try to make deals with smaller parties. The results will be known when polls close late Thursday evening.

This is the time of year when Christians around the world reflect on the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus. There are more than 2 billion Christians globally.

This year, the reflection is especially important. It comes after a tragic attack on Christian college students in Kenya. It also comes as Christians in other nations face ongoing threats. These threats include being crucified, beheaded, stoned, enslaved, sexually abused, trafficked, harassed, bombed, or forced to leave their homes. All of this happens simply because of their faith.

CNN reports that racist and offensive emails led to three city workers in Ferguson, Missouri, losing their jobs. These emails were found during a Justice Department investigation into racial prejudice in the police and court system. The messages, which were obtained by the Washington Post, contain offensive references to President Obama, the First Lady, Muslims, and minorities.

Two people have been arrested in Australia after police found at least 55 dead dogs dumped in a bushland area in Queensland. The two arrested are a 71-year-old man and a 64-year-old woman from Bundaberg. The woman is a licensed greyhound trainer. She was charged with obstructing police, while the man was charged with having an illegal firearm. The Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA) is helping police with their investigation.

Two years ago, Mike Premeau and Kathy Danke started a small frozen pizza business called Memories Gourmet Pizza Co. in Wisconsin. They sold their pizzas, including breakfast and gluten-free kinds, in stores near Green Bay and had many loyal customers.

This week, people started confusing their business with a different Memories Pizza in Indiana. That Indiana shop made news because its owners said they would not cater a same-sex wedding. Because of the mix-up, people posted angry comments on Memories Gourmet Pizza's Facebook page and called their phone number to protest.

A skeleton of a camel that was likely used by Ottoman soldiers during a siege of Vienna in the 1600s was found under a cellar in Austria. The remains were discovered in 2006 and 2007 by archaeologists from the University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna while they were digging at a construction site in Tulln. At first, the researchers thought the bones belonged to a large horse or cow. However, looking at the neck bones, jaw, and leg bones showed them that it was actually a camel.

Andrew Getty, who was 47 years old, died on Tuesday afternoon at his home in Los Angeles. His parents, Ann and Gordon Getty, released a statement saying he died of natural causes or an accident. They also asked the media and the public to respect their privacy during this sad time. The Los Angeles County coroner's office said some medication was found in his home, but they do not know if he was taking it or what his medical history was.

We might never know exactly why co-pilot Andreas Lubitz crashed Germanwings Flight 9525 into the French Alps on March 24, killing everyone on board. A new report says he sped up the plane's descent, causing the crash. It is very frightening.

As the investigation continues, we will learn more about how much Lubitz kept his mental illness a secret and how much help he got. His battle with depression raises big questions: Was he fit to fly? Should he have left his job? Should his doctors have warned people? His case highlights the difficult problems faced by people with mental illness and the stigma attached to it.

CNN Student News reported on several topics. First, they discussed news about the U.S. and Cuba. Then, they talked about California's historic drought and how it might affect the whole country. The show also mentioned a flu outbreak in Chicago, but clarified it does not affect people. Finally, they reported on a proposed tunnel project that would connect Denmark and Germany under the sea.

You can find the full transcript and sign up for the CNN Student News Roll Call on their website.

A 23-year-old man named Kamron Taylor escaped from jail in Kankakee, Illinois, on Wednesday. Sheriff Tim Bukowski said Taylor attacked a guard, stole the guard's uniform and SUV, and ran away. For several days, authorities searched for him. On Friday night, police in Chicago spotted a man matching Taylor's description. The man had the name "Gertrude" tattooed on his neck, which helped police identify him as Taylor. He was arrested overnight in Chicago.

Prince Harry, who is 30 years old, is ending his time in the military. He is going to Australia for four weeks to work with the Australian Army. He will be in Sydney, Darwin, and Perth. He has worked with Australian troops before during his 10-year career.

Three men have been charged with plotting to kill a former inmate after he was released from a Florida prison.

The men are Thomas Jordan Driver, 25; David Elliot Moran, 47; and Charles Thomas Newcomb, 42. Two of them are current or former Florida corrections officers.

An FBI informant posed as a member of the Ku Klux Klan to catch the men. The informant met the group after infiltrating a KKK branch. According to court documents, Driver told the informant that he had fought with the inmate and that he and Moran wanted him "six feet under."

Lausanne, Switzerland (CNN) -- A group of world powers called the P5+1 finished talks with Iran on Thursday about Iran's nuclear program. The agreement they made needs more work. The parties have until the end of June to finish the details. However, the talks were historic, especially for the usually tense relationship between the U.S. and Iran. The negotiations were busy and intense, but they showed how diplomacy works.

A bomb exploded near a United Nations vehicle close to the Somali city of Garowe on Monday morning. The blast killed six people, including four aid workers from UNICEF. Somalia's President called the attack "an attack against the future of our country." The attack happened about 8 a.m. in the administrative capital of the Puntland region. This follows a separate incident on Sunday where three African Union troops died in an ambush in the Lower Shabelle region. The terrorist group Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for the Monday bombing.

Prince Harry arrived in Australia on Monday. He will spend four weeks there with the military. Before he started his duty, he visited the Australian War Memorial in Canberra. He paid his respects at the Tomb of the Unknown Australian Soldier. A crowd of people watched him. Some took his photo, and a boy held a sign that said, "Red Heads Rule!" The Australian Defence Forces said Harry will live and work with the Army in Sydney, Darwin, and Perth.

Australia, a key U.S. partner, has agreed to share intelligence with Iran. Foreign Minister Julie Bishop said the agreement is a casual arrangement focused on tracking Australians fighting in Iraq. However, one lawmaker called the move "dancing with the devil." Bishop recently became the first Australian minister to visit Iran in 12 years. She met with President Hassan Rouhani, and the deal was announced during an interview she gave on Monday.

Marseille, France (CNN)Tests on the flight recorder from the downed Germanwings Flight 9525 show that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately made the plane descend faster. The "black box" was found Thursday on the mountainside in the French Alps where the plane crashed on March 24. The French air accident investigation agency, the BEA, said its team immediately started looking at the information.

A 110-day chase across the ocean ended when a ship called the Thunder sent a distress call. The ship had been wanted by Interpol for suspected fishing crimes. The crew of the Bob Barker had been following the Thunder for months. The rescue happened in the Gulf of Guinea, off the coast of west Africa.

Most days, 16-year-old Jason Zobott walks into Huntley High School in suburban Chicago around 7:30 a.m. Like other students, he starts his morning there. However, the rest of his day is different. Zobott is part of the school's blended learning program, which mixes online classes with traditional ones. About one-third of the school's 2,700 students are in this program. In 2015, the school planned to have most students learn this way. Zobott, a top student who does many activities, said the online work is easy to access. He likes that he can learn on his own.

Kenya attacked Al-Shabaab targets in Somalia with airstrikes. This happened days after an attack at Garissa University College that killed nearly 150 people. A military source said the airstrikes were part of an operation that started in 2011, and not a punishment for the university attack. The source did not give their name to the media.

Pope Francis gave a speech at the end of Easter Mass. In the speech, he reminded people that the Vatican is a state and that he is a moral diplomat. He talked about the suffering in current conflicts and asked for violence to stop. He specifically asked for an end to bloodshed in Iraq and Syria and for aid to reach people in need. He also asked the world not to ignore the tragedy and the refugees in those countries.

Students and teachers at Duke University marched on Wednesday afternoon. They were chanting, "We are not afraid. We stand together."

This happened after a noose was found hanging from a tree on campus. The noose was found near a student center at 2 a.m. Duke officials are asking anyone with information to call the police.

Photos of the noose were shared on social media, causing anger in the community. Hundreds of people gathered at a forum held on the steps of Duke Chapel, near where the noose was found. At the forum, a speaker said, "This is no Duke we will accept. This is no Duke we want. This is not the Duke we're here to experience."

A U.S. citizen named Muhanad Mahmoud Al Farekh was deported from Pakistan to the United States. He appeared in court on Thursday and is accused of planning to fight against American forces abroad. He is charged with helping terrorists, but he did not enter a plea. A CNN analyst said this is good news.

A border guard was killed in a shootout with militants in Yemen this week. This was the first publicly known death for Saudi Arabia since it started airstrikes against rebels in the country.

The fight happened Wednesday night near the border in southwestern Saudi Arabia. Militants on the Yemeni side fired first, and Saudi border guards returned fire.

Besides the guard who was killed, 10 other soldiers were hurt, but their injuries were not life-threatening. The slain guard was identified as Cpl. Salman Ali Yahya al-Maliki.

I am a CNN reporter going to a camel race in Dubai. I am the only Gulf national on the team, so people expect me to know about this old tradition. Even though I tried to wear the local dress, I still feel like an outsider.

A happy farm owner takes me to the majlis, where the camel owners are sitting. It is a large, fancy room. The owners are sitting on the floor and eating a dish called a'aish, which is fish and rice. The conversation is loud and exciting.

Havana, Cuba (CNN)Charlie Hill sits in a dark bar on a sunny Havana day. "Hey man," he says with a raspy voice and a nod. He knows people have been looking for him for a long time. For 43 years, Cuba has protected him from charges that he killed a New Mexico police officer and hijacked a plane to Havana. Now 65, Hill decided to talk to CNN after they tried to reach him for two years. He wants to discuss how, for the first time, he is thinking about leaving Cuba and returning to the United States.

Misao Okawa, who was 117 years old, has died. She was the oldest person in the world.

Okawa died on Wednesday morning in Osaka, Japan. She was born on March 5, 1898. Her family ran a kimono shop. She is survived by three children, four grandchildren, and six great-grandchildren.

A worker at the nursing home where she lived said Okawa had a mild personality and loved to eat. Her favorite foods were sushi and udon noodles. She had eaten a lot of cake the day before she died, which was her birthday.

Washington (CNN) - As the Missouri National Guard prepared to go to Ferguson to help stop riots that happened last year, the guard used military words like "enemy" and "adversaries" to describe the protesters. The guard went to Ferguson to help police, whom many community leaders and civil rights activists said used too much force and made a bad situation worse. The protests started in August and continued sporadically until the end of the year.

Gunmen attacked the education ministry in Mogadishu, Somalia, on Tuesday. A suicide car bombing happened first at the entrance, and then five gunmen entered the building and started shooting. At least 12 people were killed and 16 were injured. The Islamist group Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for the attack.

Gregory Margolin is now 87 years old. He was a 16-year-old Jewish recruit in the Soviet Red Army during World War II. He fought the Nazis, but his family had to flee. He says he did not show that he was Jewish because people were being killed everywhere. This year, in Ukraine, he found himself in war again. Margolin was a sniper and later a commander. He still wears his old military uniform with medals. His granddaughter Liora is amazed that he survived the war.

In Chibok, northeastern Nigeria, more than 200 schoolgirls were kidnapped from their boarding school dormitories exactly one year ago. They are still missing. This event happened because fanatical thugs attacked the school in the dead of night. The Nigerian government and the rest of the world have been criticized for failing to protect the girls and for not paying enough attention to their disappearance.

In Norway, digital radio is replacing FM radio. By 2027, Norway will be the first country in the world to stop using FM radio completely. However, this does not mean people will have no radio; they will just switch to digital. Officials say many of the country's 5 million people have already made the change. On FM, listeners can only find five stations, but on digital radio, there are twenty. Half the country already listens to digital radio, said Culture Minister Thorhild Widvey.

Everybody loves a good comeback story, especially one about a big dinosaur. For over a century, scientists had removed the Brontosaurus from their books. However, a new study suggests that the Brontosaurus is different enough to have its own name. O.C. Marsh first named the dinosaur in 1879 after he found 25 crates of bones in Wyoming. The Brontosaurus was similar to, but smaller than, the Apatosaurus. Marsh chose the name "Brontosaurus," which means "thunder lizard."

Al Qaeda in Yemen is offering a reward of 20 kilograms of gold to anyone who kills or captures two men. The men are Abdelmalik Bedrudin Al-Houthi, a rebel leader who took over Yemen's capital, and former President Ali Abdullah Saleh. The gold is worth about $774,000. Al Qaeda called the two men the "two heads of evil."

Before landing a gyrocopter on the Capitol lawn Wednesday, Doug Hughes wrote about his intentions and the reasons behind them on a website called thedemocracyclub.org. The 61-year-old Florida postal carrier wrote in an online post titled "Your Pilot" that the point of the flight was to spotlight corruption in Washington, D.C., and present solutions to institutional graft. He made it clear that his flight was not a secret. Before he took off, he sent an email to info@barackobama.com. In the letter, he tried to persuade the guardians of the Capitol that he was not a threat and that shooting him down would be a bigger headache than letting him deliver letters to Congress.

Bad news for Rio de Janeiro before the 2016 Olympics continued on Monday. Scores of dead fish were found in the Rodrigo de Freitas lagoon. With just over a year until the Games start, the legislative assembly of Rio de Janeiro began an investigation into why the fish died. They will work with the State Environmental Institute and the Secretariat of State for the Environment to look into the deaths in other lakes and bays as well.

Anthony Ray Hinton is 58 years old. But in many ways, he is new to the world -- at least the one we know. Little things like using a fork, going out at night, and tucking into bed without anyone checking on him are all strange for someone like Hinton, who spent nearly 30 years on Alabama's death row.

Until one week ago, when his murder convictions were wiped clean, Hinton walked out of a county jail in Birmingham. "I have to pinch myself to tell myself that I'm free," he told CNN's Brooke Baldwin on Friday. "It's going to take a little time, but I'll get used to it."

A poll about the UK election debate between seven party leaders found no clear winner. The results were very close.

Comres for ITV had Conservative David Cameron, Labour's Ed Miliband, and UK Independence Party leader Nigel Farage tied in first place with 21% each. Scottish National Party leader Nicola Sturgeon was close behind with 20%.

Another poll by ICM for The Guardian gave Labour's Ed Miliband the highest score with 25. Conservative David Cameron came second with 24, while UK Independence Party leader Nigel Farage got 19 and Sturgeon got 17.

A New York judge has ruled that Facebook is an acceptable way to serve divorce papers. Ellanora Arthur Baidoo has been trying to divorce her husband, Victor Sena Blood-Dzraku, for several years. Her lawyer says they could not find him to give him the papers in person. Baidoo has spoken to her husband on the phone, and he told her he has no fixed address and no job.

It sounds like a science fiction movie. A person has a terrible accident and ends up in the hospital, brain dead and on life support. Doctors ask the family about organ donation, but instead of saving up to eight lives, the family is asked to donate the whole body to save just one person. Perhaps a quadriplegic whose mind is stronger than their broken body. Although this sounds crazy, Italian doctor Sergio Canavero says we are getting close to doing a head transplant. He calls this project HEAVEN, which stands for head anastomosis venture; anastomosis is the medical term for surgically connecting two parts.
